facts.headline: Venice's patron saint arrived hidden in a barrel of pork
facts.body_html: According to legend, two Venetian merchants smuggled the body of St. Mark the Evangelist out of Alexandria in 828 AD by hiding it under a layer of pork and cabbage — Muslim customs inspectors, forbidden from touching pork, let the crates straight through.

facts.headline: This bridge's shops were built to pay for it
facts.body_html: The stone Rialto Bridge, completed in 1591 after designs by Michelangelo and Palladio were rejected, has rows of shops lining both sides — their rent helped cover the cost of building and maintaining it, a model used since the 1400s.
suggested_queries: Ponte di Rialto Venice Grand Canal

facts.headline: Condemned prisoners took their last look at Venice through this window
facts.body_html: The enclosed Bridge of Sighs, built around 1600 to link the Doge's Palace to its prison, got its name from the legend that condemned men sighed at their final glimpse of the city through its small stone-grilled windows.

facts.headline: A 1562 law is why every gondola in Venice is black
facts.body_html: Venetian nobles once competed to build the most extravagant gondolas — until a 1562 sumptuary law ordered every gondola painted plain black to curb the showing-off. The rule is still followed today.
suggested_queries: Venice gondola Grand Canal black boats

facts.headline: 78 underwater gates now hold back the sea for this city
facts.body_html: Venice sinks a couple of millimeters a year while the sea around it rises — in 2020, the city activated MOSE, a system of 78 mobile floodgates on the seafloor that rise to seal off the lagoon during high tides, keeping St. Mark's Square dry for the first time in years.

facts.headline: Masks let every Venetian pretend to be equal for one season
facts.body_html: Venice's Carnival masks trace back centuries and let nobles and commoners mingle anonymously, erasing class lines for the length of the festival — some styles, like the beak-nosed plague doctor mask, started out as protective gear centuries earlier.

facts.headline: This city of 118 islands has no cars at all
facts.body_html: Venice is built across 118 small islands linked by roughly 400 bridges, with canals and footpaths standing in for streets — making it Europe's largest car-free urban area.
